name: El Cadejo
description: A Central American spirit that takes the form of a large dog, appearing in two opposing variants: a benevolent white cadejo that protects nocturnal travellers and a malevolent black cadejo (sometimes identified with the Devil) that harms them.
full_description: El Cadejo (Spanish, sometimes 'el Cadejos' in Costa Rica) is a supernatural dog of Central American folklore, present across Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama, and several Mexican states. It appears in two opposing variants: a white cadejo that protects travellers — particularly drunkards — through the night, and a black cadejo (sometimes equated with the Devil) that attempts to harm them. The creature is described as a large, shaggy, dog- or wolf-like animal of cow-like size, with glowing red eyes when aggressive and blue eyes when calm; common features include goat hooves, dragging chains, and an intense goat-like odour. In Costa Rica and Panama only the malevolent (black) form is recognised. Folkloric protection includes religious phrases and crossing oneself, with a regional formula recorded as 'con permiso, compadre Alejo'. The legend is widely understood as a syncretic complex blending Spanish colonial Catholicism with pre-Columbian Mesoamerican beliefs about naguales (animal spiritual doubles), in which the dog occupied a sacred psychopomp role guiding the dead.
origin: Folkloric range across Central America (Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua, Costa Rica, Panama) with extensions into several Mexican states.

etymology.origin: Spanish 'cadejo' is recorded in regional dictionaries as a tangle or skein (of hair, fibre); the folkloric figure's name may evoke the matted, shaggy appearance of the creature. The underlying mythological substrate draws on Maya and Nahua nahualism.
etymology.meaning: Folkloric: the shaggy/tangled dog-like spirit. Lexical: 'tangle' (rope, hair).
etymology.first_use: Present in 19th-century Central American folklore collections; standardised in 20th-century compilations such as those of Salarrué and Sergio Ramírez.

timeline.event: Salvadoran writer Salarrué (Salvador Salazar Arrué) publishes 'Cuentos de barro', helping to canonise cadejo narratives in literary form
timeline.significance: Influential literary preservation of Salvadoran cadejo folklore

timeline.event: Sergio Ramírez and other Central American writers continue to anthologise cadejo material in regional collections
timeline.significance: Ongoing literary engagement with the figure

related.name: Black Dog
related.description: British folkloric large black dog spirit (Black Shuck, Barghest, etc.)

cultural_notes: Looking the black cadejo in the eye, turning one's back, or speaking to it is held to risk madness; protection is sought through prayer, the sign of the cross, and regional formulas.

sources.title: Por los viejos barrios de la Ciudad de Guatemala
